title: The Morning Call That Told Richard Eu His Family Firm Had Been Sold
dek: Soon after taking charge of his great-grandfather's medicine business, Richard Eu learned relatives had sold it, and chose to stay on.

story.event: Losing the family medicine business to a takeover, staying on, and buying it back with his cousins
story.summary: Soon after Richard Eu became general manager of Eu Yan Sang, the traditional Chinese medicine business founded by his great-grandfather Eu Kong in Gopeng in 1879, relatives sold their shares and the Singapore company Lum Chang took majority control. Eu stayed on, and in 1993 he and his cousins bought the business back, forming Eu Yan Sang International, which listed in Singapore in 2000.
paragraphs: At half past eight one morning, soon after Richard Eu had become general manager of Eu Yan Sang at the end of 1989, the phone rang. It was a merchant bank: "We have just received a notice of takeover from Lum Chang." The Singapore company now held more than half the shares. Eu later remembered the shock, and not knowing what would happen next.

By the company's account, the business began in 1879, when his great-grandfather, Eu Kong, opened a Chinese medicine shop in Gopeng, a tin-mining town in Perak, for miners who used opium to dull their pain. Eu Kong's son, Eu Tong Sen, built it into a chain. After Tong Sen died at the start of the Second World War, his heirs faced heavy death duties and sold most of what he had left. By Richard Eu's account, Eu Yan Sang was the last family business standing, its shares spread among dozens of relatives. When an uncle retired at 70 with no successor, Eu, then in his early forties after years in banking and finance, put himself forward. Some uncles, he said, were jealous and arranged a sale.

Lum Chang, as he understood it, did not want the medicine business. It wanted the company's other assets and its stock-market listing, and it kept him on and gave the family first right to buy the shares back when it was ready to sell. He stayed. The sale was not the hardest part, he told KiniBiz; harder was working out the right direction for a business many regarded as belonging to the past.

In 1993 Eu and his cousins bought the business back from Lum Chang, using their own and borrowed money and keeping the older generation out of running it. They formed Eu Yan Sang International, which listed in Singapore in 2000. Eu set about making Chinese medicine easier to understand, explaining why a remedy was meant to help instead of asking customers to take it on trust. When he stepped down as chief executive in 2017, the company had more than 200 shops.

quote.text: Who can (make) the muddy water (clear)? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear. Who can secure the condition of rest? Let movement go on, and the condition of rest will gradually arise.
quote.source_title: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics, tr. James Legge, Project Gutenberg eBook #216
quote.connection: After the takeover call, Eu did not leave. He kept working inside a company he no longer controlled until the way back opened. Laozi pairs stillness with movement: muddy water clears when it is left alone, and rest arrives while work goes on.

reflection: The worst part of Eu's morning was not knowing. A phone call had changed who owned the work he had just taken on, and nothing about the next step was clear yet. What he did first was ordinary: he stayed, kept working, and learned what the new owners actually wanted.

When news knocks the ground from under you, the urge is to decide everything at once, often while you are still shaken. Laozi suggests letting the water settle first. You can keep doing the next plain task while it does, and make the larger decision on a calmer day, when you can see the bottom again.
invitation: If something this week has stirred you up, write down the one decision it seems to demand, and set a day, at least two nights' sleep away, on which you will make it.

sources.title: Modernizing Family Legacy Through The Times with Richard Eu

sources.supports: The 8.30 a.m. call from the merchant bank and its words; Lum Chang holding over 50%; the shock and uncertainty; his uncle retiring at 70 and Eu putting himself forward; some uncles 'very jealous' organising a sellout to Lum Chang; Lum Chang wanting other assets and the listing, not the medicine business, and giving the family first right to buy back; Lum Chang keeping its promise; the buyout by Eu and his cousins with their own money, leveraged, and leaving the older generation out; death duties after his grandfather died at the outbreak of the Second World War forcing sales, leaving Eu Yan Sang as the only family business; the founding as healthcare for opium-dependent miners in Gopeng; his work as general manager from 1989 to retirement as group CEO in 2017; over 200 retail stores

sources.title: Keeping the family dream alive
sources.supports: Eu Kong's arrival in 1873 and the first Yan Sang shop in Gopeng in 1879 for tin miners who depended on opium, as told by the company; Eu's role as alternate director to his father; his uncle retiring at 70 with no successor; Eu joining as general manager at the end of 1989; the acquisition by Lum Chang soon after; the 1993 buyout with his cousins forming Eu Yan Sang International Holdings, listed in Singapore in 2000; his remark that the sale was traumatic but the new owners kept him on, and that the harder part was finding the right direction for the business

sources.title: Richard Eu: Eu Yan Sang
sources.supports: Eu joined in 1989 when traditional Chinese medicine was widely seen as a 'sunset' industry; stakes dispersed across more than seventy family members; his career in banking and finance before joining; his aim of explaining why products work rather than relying on 'myth and mystery'; his retirement as CEO at 70

research_notes: Change of episode: the slate asked for Eu Kong opening the Gopeng shop in 1879. That founding is told consistently by the company, the National Library Board (BiblioAsia) and the National Heritage Board (Roots), but no account in Eu Kong's own words was found, and other accounts drawing on Ilsa Sharp's 2009 biography of Eu Tong Sen (Path of the Righteous Crane), seen here only through a blog, Ipoh World's local-history database and Wikipedia, describe a more mixed beginning: arrival in 1876 rather than 1873, a grocery business that later added a dispensary, and Eu Kong becoming a government revenue farmer in Gopeng (Wikipedia, citing Sharp, says the family's revenue farms included opium). Because that disagreement goes to the heart of the 1879 story and could not be checked against the biography itself, the edition tells a different, better-documented episode of the same company, in which the protagonist speaks for himself, and gives the founding only as 'by the company's account'. Dates and ages: KiniBiz has Eu saying he joined at the end of 1989; Wikipedia's Richard Eu article says 1990; the story uses the end of 1989. Endeavor's write-up calls him 40 at the time, but he was born in 1947 (Wikipedia; HNWorth says he turned 70 on stepping down in 2017), so the story says 'early forties'. Takeover date: KiniBiz says 'not long after' he joined; Wikipedia says 1990. The 'jealous' uncles and Lum Chang's motives are Eu's own account and are attributed. HNWorth's mention of a 1992 Hong Kong listing refers, per KiniBiz, to Eu Yan Sang (Hong Kong); the story does not use it. Shop numbers vary by source and year: over 200 (Endeavor 2022, Roots), around 300 retail outlets and 33 clinics (HNWorth 2018), 170 outlets (Wikipedia, current); the story uses the conservative 'more than 200'. Death of Eu Tong Sen: 1941 (Wikipedia); Endeavor says at the outbreak of the Second World War. Funding is 'mixed': the company was publicly listed, and the 1993 buyout used the cousins' own and borrowed money. NLB Infopedia's Eu Yan Sang entry did not load for automated requests and is not cited; the Inquirer and other reprints were blocked. The Laozi passage describes the ancient masters of the Tao; it is applied here by analogy.
